subject: ENGLISH LANGUAGE
title: Reading: Reading Fluency
overview: Fluent reading is accurate, steady and full of expression, so the listener can follow the meaning. In this sub-strand you will use fluency strategies on a farm text of about 300 words, answer questions that ask you to read between the lines, and bring a short script and a rhyme to life with your voice.

lessons.title: Reading a farm text with accuracy and expression
objectives: Read a text of about 300 words accurately and at a steady speed.
Use phrasing, expression and repeated reading.
Explain why fluent reading helps understanding.
lessons.intro: A learner who gallops through a page may say every word and still miss the story. Another learner who stops dead at each word never lets the sentences join up. Fluency is the middle path: accurate, steady and meaningful.
lessons.notes:
### Three parts of fluency
**Accuracy** means you say the words that are really on the page. Guessing harvest when the word is fertilizer changes the facts.

**Rate** means a reasonable speed. Read fast enough for the sentence to sound like speech, and slowly enough for you and your listener to understand. If you race, meaning drops out. If you halt on every word, the story breaks into pieces.

**Expression** means your voice shows the sense. Let your voice fall at a full stop, pause briefly at a comma, and sound interested when something new happens. A question lifts a little at the end.

### Strategies that help
- Look ahead to the end of the phrase, not only at the next letter.
- Read in groups of words: met us at the gate, not met / us / at / the / gate.
- If you stumble, go back to the start of the phrase and try once more.
- Read the same paragraph three times. The third reading is usually smoother. This is called repeated reading.
- When you read from a screen, use a site or file an adult has chosen, and do not click away to unknown links.

Fluency matters because understanding rides on it. A listener cannot picture the tractor, the pests or the meal if the words are scrambled or too fast.

### A Saturday on the Farm
Last Saturday our class visited a farm near the school. The farmer, Mrs Achieng, met us at the gate and asked us to walk slowly so that we would not frighten the hens. She wore boots because the path was wet. First she showed us the vegetable field. Rows of sukuma wiki, tomatoes and onions stood in straight lines. She said the plants need water, sunlight and good soil. A boy asked why some leaves had holes. Mrs Achieng explained that pests such as caterpillars chew leaves. She does not spray carelessly. She picks some pests off by hand and grows indigenous vegetables that do well in our climate.

Next we watched the tractor. It pulled a plough that turned the soil in long brown lines. The driver told us never to run near a moving tractor. We stood behind the fence and only looked. In the shed we saw sacks of seed, a watering can and a wheelbarrow. A girl pointed at a bag of fertilizer. Mrs Achieng said fertilizer feeds the soil, but a farmer must use the right amount. Too much can wash into a river and harm the life in the water.

At noon we sat under a tree and ate mangoes the farm had harvested that morning. They were ripe and sweet. While we ate, Mrs Achieng told us to wash fruit and vegetables before we eat them. Those foods, with grains and beans, help the body grow. On the way home we sang a rhyme about seeds and rain. I wrote three new words in my book: harvest, pests and plough. The visit taught me that food does not appear in the market by itself. Someone plants it, protects it and gathers it with care. We thanked Mrs Achieng before we left.

On a first reading, mark two words you need to look at again. On the second reading, keep those words smooth. On the third, read a paragraph aloud to a partner and ask, Could you picture the farm?

keyWords.meaning: reading accurately, at a suitable speed and with expression
reading the words that are actually written
using your voice to show the meaning and the punctuation
reading the same text several times so it becomes smoother

examples.problem: A learner reads fertilizer as factory. What part of fluency has slipped?
steps: The word on the page was not the word that was said.
That is a problem of accuracy, even if the speed was fine.

examples.problem: Where should the voice pause in this sentence? She wore boots because the path was wet.
steps: There is no comma in the middle.
The voice falls and pauses at the full stop.
examples.answer: At the full stop after wet

activity.title: Three readings
materials: The passage A Saturday on the Farm
steps: Read the passage silently and underline two words you want to practise.
Read one paragraph aloud at a steady speed. A partner follows on the page and notes any word that was changed.
Read the same paragraph again with expression, pausing at full stops.
Tell your partner one fact you understood better on the second reading.

practice.question: Name the three parts of fluent reading.
practice.answer: Accuracy, a reasonable speed, and expression.

practice.question: Why did some leaves in the field have holes?
practice.answer: Pests such as caterpillars had chewed them.

practice.question: What did the driver tell the class about the tractor?
practice.answer: Never to run near a moving tractor.

practice.question: Why does reading the same paragraph again help?
practice.answer: Repeated reading makes the words more accurate and the voice smoother, so the meaning is easier to follow.

summary: Fluent reading is accurate, steady and expressive.
Phrase words in groups, pause at full stops, and reread.
Fluency helps both the reader and the listener understand the text.

lessons.title: Reader's theatre, rhythm and inference
objectives: Read a part in a reader's theatre with a lively voice.
Keep the rhythm of a short rhyme.
Answer direct questions and questions that need an inference.
lessons.intro: In a reader's theatre you do not need costumes or a stage. You need the words and a voice that makes a listener see the farm. The script below is for that kind of reading.
lessons.notes:
### Direct questions and inferences
A **direct question** is answered in the words of the text. Who met the class at the gate? Mrs Achieng. The sentence says so.

An **inference** is a conclusion you draw from clues. The text may not state it in one ready sentence. Why did the class stay behind the fence? The driver had warned them never to run near a moving tractor, and the next sentence says they stood behind the fence and only looked. The clue is safety. Why wear boots? The path was wet. What does the writer mean by saying food does not appear in the market by itself? Someone has to plant, protect and harvest it.

When you answer, use a clue from the text and then say what it shows. I know they were careful because they stood behind the fence.

### Reader's theatre
Take turns. Narrator reads the story line. The other parts speak as people.

Narrator: Mrs Achieng met the class at the gate.
Mrs Achieng: Walk slowly. The hens are easily frightened. The path is wet, so step carefully.
Narrator: In the field, a boy pointed at the leaves.
Boy: Why are there holes in these leaves?
Mrs Achieng: Pests have been chewing them. I pick many off by hand. I do not spray carelessly.
Narrator: The tractor pulled the plough.
Driver: Stay behind the fence. Never run near a moving tractor.
Narrator: At noon they ate fruit under a tree.
Mrs Achieng: Wash the fruit and vegetables before you eat them.
Narrator: The class thanked her and left.

Speak so that the warning sounds like a warning and the welcome sounds like a welcome. Look up from the page at the end of a sentence.

### Rhythm in a rhyme
Clap once for each strong beat as you read.

Seed in the soil, rain on the row,
Leaves lift up and the seedlings grow.
Wash what you pick, and share what you know,
Thank the farmer who ploughs the row.

The lines are similar in length, and row, grow, know and row rhyme. Keeping that pattern is another kind of fluent reading. You can sing the rhyme to any simple tune you already know, as long as the words stay clear.

If you listen to a recording, echo one line at a time, then join the lines. Fluent readers sound confident because the words are ready in the mouth. That confidence is built by practice, not by shouting.

keyWords.meaning: reading a script aloud in parts, using voices instead of costumes or a stage
a conclusion you draw from clues in the text
a repeated beat or pattern in a poem or song

examples.problem: Is this a direct question or an inference? What fruit did the class eat at noon?
steps: Look for the exact food in the passage.
The text says they ate mangoes.
examples.answer: A direct question. The answer is mangoes.

examples.problem: Why did the writer thank the people who plant and harvest, not only the market?
steps: The last lines say food does not appear by itself.
Someone plants it, protects it and gathers it.
examples.answer: Because farmers do the work that brings food to the market.

activity.title: Voices on the farm
steps: In groups, give out the parts: Narrator, Mrs Achieng, Boy and Driver.
Practise once for accuracy and a second time for expression. No costumes are needed.
After the performance, each group answers one direct question and one inference question from the passage.
Clap and read the rhyme together, keeping the rhythm steady.

practice.question: Who explained the holes in the leaves?
Why did the class stand behind the fence instead of running beside the tractor?
practice.answer: The driver told them never to run near a moving tractor, so they stayed in a safe place.

practice.question: What is a reader's theatre?
practice.answer: Reading a script aloud in parts and using your voice to bring it to life, without a set or costumes.

practice.question: Which words rhyme with row in the farm rhyme?

summary: A direct question is answered on the page. An inference uses clues.
A reader's theatre builds fluency through expressive voices.
Rhythm and rhyme give the voice a steady pattern to follow.

quiz.question: Fluent reading includes accuracy, expression and ________.
quiz.explanation: Rate, or a reasonable speed, is the third part of fluency beside accuracy and expression.

quiz.question: What should you do when you stumble on a phrase?
options: Go back to the start of the phrase and try again
quiz.explanation: Returning to the start of the phrase repairs the mistake without breaking the meaning.

quiz.question: Why is repeated reading useful?
options: The text usually becomes more accurate and smoother
It removes the need to understand
quiz.explanation: Reading the same text again helps accuracy, pace and expression.

quiz.question: Which crop was NOT named in the vegetable field?
quiz.explanation: Mangoes were the fruit eaten at noon. The field had sukuma wiki, tomatoes and onions.

quiz.question: What can happen if too much fertilizer is used?
options: It always makes fruit sweeter the same day
It can wash into a river and harm the life in the water
It removes the need to plant
quiz.explanation: Mrs Achieng says too much fertilizer can wash into a river and harm the life in the water.

quiz.question: Why did Mrs Achieng wear boots?
quiz.explanation: The text says she wore boots because the path was wet.

quiz.question: The class stood behind the fence. What can you infer?
options: They were hiding from the farmer
They were obeying the driver and staying safe
The tractor was inside the shed
They did not want any fruit
quiz.explanation: The driver had just warned them not to run near the moving tractor.

quiz.question: Food does not appear in the market by itself. What does the writer mean?
quiz.answer: Someone has to plant, protect and harvest the food before it can be sold.
quiz.explanation: The next sentence says someone plants it, protects it and gathers it with care.

quiz.question: What does a reader's theatre need most?
options: Voices that bring the script to life
quiz.explanation: A reader's theatre uses expressive reading. It does not need a set or costumes.

quiz.question: Why does fluent reading help comprehension?
quiz.answer: When the words are accurate and the pace is steady, the reader and the listener can follow the meaning.
quiz.explanation: Understanding is lost if words are wrong or the voice rushes or stalls.
